In 1837 and 1838 reformers in the British colonies of Lower Canada, now Quebec, and Upper Canada, now Ontario, rose in arms against rule by appointed governors and small elites. Both risings were quickly crushed.

In Lower Canada the Patriotes, led by Louis-Joseph Papineau, fought British troops at Saint-Denis and Saint-Charles. In Upper Canada William Lyon Mackenzie led a march on Toronto. Leaders fled to the United States; some rebels were hanged and others transported to Australia.

Britain sent Lord Durham to report. He urged uniting the two colonies, which was done in 1840, hoping to absorb the French Canadians, and granting responsible government, achieved in 1848. The path led to Confederation in 1867, while the Patriotes fed Quebec nationalism and memories of the Acadian and 1759 defeats.
